description_full: Torex Resources Inc., a precious metals mining company, engages in the acquisition, exploration, and development of mineral properties in Mexico and the United States. The company explores gold, copper, silver, and carbon deposits. Its flagship project is a 100% owned Morelos Complex covering an area of 29,000 hectares located in Guerrero, Mexico. Torex Resources Inc. was formerly known as Torex Gold Resources Inc. and changed its name to Torex Resources Inc. in October 2026. Torex Resources Inc. was incorporated in 1980 and is based in Toronto, Canada.
ceo_bio: Mr. Andrew P. Snowden C.A., C.P.A. | President, CEO & Director | Compensation: $732,218 (FY2025)
financial_summary: Torex Resources Inc. is a mid-cap basic materials business with a $4.5B market cap on $1.3B of annual revenue.

The top line has compounded at +15% over the past three years, the kind of sustained demand persistence that marks a compounder. Operating margins are expanding by +3.2pp year-over-year, which is one of the strongest signals that the moat is deepening.
Returns on capital run at 19% against a 9% cost of capital — a 10-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat, with gross margins sitting at 38%.

The business throws off $135M in free cash flow — roughly 10 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.21× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 0.0× net debt/EBITDA, and interest coverage of 74× is fortress-like.

Shareholder yield is only 1.0%, a thin return of capital, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and within its sector the business captures 3.1× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

sect: Its 41% operating margin runs 31pp above the Basic Materials median (9%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It captures 3.11x its revenue share in sector profits, taking a disproportionate slice of the profit pool.
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 222 companies in the universe; the top four hold 25% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are roughly flat over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 21% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 61% and a beta of 0.92, it moves roughly with the market, though its beta has shifted (1y 1.84 vs 5y 0.85), so read it loosely.
About $1.6M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 56% in the 2022 bear market.
val: The stock trades only 11% below its DCF fair value of $55.58, a thin margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 21%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $20.93 to $156 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
Multiples send mixed signals against Basic Materials peers: cheaper on P/E 7.2 vs 15.4 and EV/EBITDA 3.7 vs 7.9, richer on P/FCF 33.1 vs 21.8 (sector median).
Earnings yields are mixed: an FCF yield of 3.0% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 12.2% (vs the 8% bar).
The price implies 14.7% annual cash-flow growth, 2pp less than the model expects.
prof: ROIC of 19% clears the cost of capital of 9.0% by 10pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have been steady (CV 0.17).
It runs a 38% gross margin and converts 10% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: a Piotroski score of 7/9 and cash conversion of 1.21x.
ROE of 17% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (1.2x equity multiplier).
SG&A jumped 47% last year, worth watching.
hlth: Leverage is conservative at 0.0x net debt to EBITDA ($119.5M of cash against $133.2M of debt), with interest covered 73.6x.
Warning signs: a Beneish M-score that flags possible earnings manipulation.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 14.6% over 3 years.
At current returns, reinvesting 55% of profits supports about 10.7% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.4%), and institutions hold 72%.
Shareholder yield is a modest 1.0% (0.8% in buybacks and 0.9% in dividends).
